unit.title: Forces and magnetism
unit.blurb: Gravity, satellites, friction, balanced forces and magnets that attract and repel.

O1.t: Describe gravity, normal forces and applied forces, and measure forces in newtons.

O2.t: Explain that gravity keeps the Moon and artificial satellites in orbit.

O3.t: Describe friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust.

O4.t: Describe balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects on movement.

O5.t: Sort materials into magnetic and non-magnetic, and know that most metals are not magnetic.

O6.t: Describe magnetic poles, attraction and repulsion, and magnetic fields; compare magnet strength fairly.

captions: Hello, force fans! Hold on to your seats!
This is lesson 5.1: gravity, normal forces and applied forces.
Kick a ball high into the sky.
What happens? It always comes back down. It never floats away.
That is because the Earth is pulling it. This pull is a force called gravity.
Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth: you, your bag, an apple, even the Moon!
We measure forces in newtons, using a forcemeter. The pull of gravity on something is its weight.
Gravity is pulling you down right now. So why don't you sink through the floor?
Because the floor pushes back up on you! This upward push from a surface is called the normal force.
The two forces are balanced, so you stay still. Phew!
Pause and think. What is the push of a surface on an object called?
When you push or pull something yourself, you use an applied force.
Pushing a shopping trolley is an applied force. So is pulling a door open.
And lifting a heavy box is an applied force too. Bend your knees!
Scientists draw forces as arrows.
The arrow points the way the force acts.
A longer arrow means a bigger force.
Riddle time! What is the most attractive thing on Earth? It never lets you go!
Gravity, of course!
Your turn. Which way does gravity pull?
Let's measure some forces.
Hook a forcemeter onto a bag, and lift it slowly. Read the scale in newtons.
Try other objects, like a pencil case, a book and a shoe.
Which one needs the biggest force to lift?
Let's remember.
Gravity pulls things towards the centre of the Earth.
The normal force is a surface pushing back up.
Applied forces are the pushes and pulls we make.
And forces are measured in newtons.
Forceful work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, space cadets! Three, two, one… blast off!
This is lesson 5.2: gravity and satellites.
A satellite is an object that moves around a planet. Its path is called an orbit.
The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite.
Artificial satellites are made by people. They help with phones, television, weather forecasts and maps.
So why don't satellites fall to the ground?
Gravity is pulling them towards the Earth all the time.
But they are also moving forwards very fast. They keep falling around the Earth, and never hit it!
Pause and think. What keeps a satellite in its orbit?
Here is a way to feel it. Swing a soft ball round and round on a string, outside.
The string keeps pulling the ball towards your hand, just like gravity.
If you let go, the ball flies off in a straight line. Without gravity, the Moon would do the same!
Did you know? The International Space Station goes all the way around the Earth about sixteen times every day.
The astronauts see sixteen sunrises a day. Good morning, again!
Gravity works across space. The Earth's gravity holds the Moon in its orbit.
The Sun's gravity holds all the planets in their orbits.
And the Moon's gravity pulls on the sea, making the tides go in and out.
Your turn. What is the Earth's natural satellite?
Let's go satellite spotting.
On a clear evening, go outside with an adult, and look up.
A satellite looks like a bright dot moving smoothly. It does not flash like a plane.
Count how many you can see in fifteen minutes.
Let's remember.
A satellite is an object that orbits a planet.
The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite.
Gravity keeps satellites in their orbits.
And the Sun's gravity holds the planets in theirs.
Out of this world! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, speed scientists! Let's slow things down.
This is lesson 5.3: friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust.
Run in your socks on a shiny floor, and you slide. Whee!
Put on trainers, and they grip. Trainers make more friction.
Friction is a force between two surfaces rubbing together. It slows things down, or stops them sliding.
Pause and think. Which makes more friction on a floor, socks or trainers?
Drop a flat sheet of paper. It floats down slowly.
Now scrunch the same paper into a ball and drop it. It falls much faster!
Air pushes against moving things. This is air resistance. A parachute has a huge surface, to catch lots of air.
Try running in a swimming pool. It is hard work! Water pushes back. This is water resistance.
Fish and boats have smooth, pointed shapes, called streamlined shapes, to slip through easily.
Water also pushes up on things. This upward push is called upthrust. It helps ducks and boats float.
Did you know? A cheetah's claws grip the ground like football boots.
Lots of friction means it can turn super fast without slipping!
Joke time! Why are parachutes always so calm?
Because they never rush. They take it slow!
Your turn. What is the upward push of water called?
Let's test friction with shoes.
Put a shoe on a tray, and slowly lift one end.
Measure how high the tray is when the shoe starts to slide.
Test different shoes. The higher you can lift the tray, the more grip the shoe has.
Let's remember.
Friction acts between surfaces, and slows things down.
Air resistance pushes against things moving through air.
Water resistance pushes against things moving through water.
And upthrust is the upward push of water.
Smooth work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, force fans! Let's add up some forces.
This is lesson 5.4: multiple forces.
Most things have more than one force acting on them.
In a tug of war, if both teams pull equally hard, the forces are balanced.
Nothing changes. The rope stays still.
Now one team pulls harder.
The forces are unbalanced, so the rope moves towards the stronger team.

captions: Hello, magnet masters! Prepare to be amazed.
This is lesson 5.5: magnets and magnetic materials.
A magnet can pull some things towards it, without even touching them. Like magic, but it is science!
Look. The paper clip jumps to the magnet. So does the iron nail. But the coin, the plastic spoon and the wood stay where they are.
Materials that a magnet attracts are magnetic. Iron and steel are the most common ones. Nickel and cobalt are magnetic too.
Everything else is non-magnetic, like plastic, wood, glass and paper. And here is the surprise: most metals are not magnetic! Copper, aluminium, gold and silver are not attracted.
Pause and think. Is every metal magnetic?
Magnets help us every day. Fridge doors have magnetic strips to keep them shut.
At recycling centres, giant magnets pull steel cans out of the rubbish.
And a compass needle is a tiny magnet that always points north. Explorers use it so they don't get lost!
Joke time! What did one magnet say to the other magnet?
I find you very attractive!
Did you know? The Earth is like a giant magnet.
Some birds can sense its magnetism, and use it like a compass to fly thousands of kilometres!
Your turn. Which of these is magnetic: copper, iron or plastic?
Let's go on a magnet hunt.
Collect ten small objects, like a key, a coin, a pencil and a paper clip. Predict which ones are magnetic.
Test each one with a magnet.
Sort them into two groups. Were your predictions right?
Let's remember.
Magnets attract magnetic materials, without touching them.
Iron and steel are magnetic.
But most metals, like copper and aluminium, are not.
And plastic, wood and glass are non-magnetic.

captions: Hello again, magnet masters! Let's feel the force.
This is lesson 5.6: magnetic force.
Every magnet has two ends, called poles: a north pole and a south pole.
Bring a north pole near a south pole. Click! They attract, or pull together.
But bring two south poles together, and they push apart. They repel. Opposite poles attract, and like poles repel.
Pause and think. What happens when two north poles meet?
Here is a cool trick. Slide some ring magnets onto a pencil.
Turn them so that like poles face each other.
They repel so strongly that they float in the air! Some super-fast trains use magnets to float above the track.
The space around a magnet where it pushes or pulls is called its magnetic field.
Sprinkle iron filings around a magnet, and they line up to show the field. It is strongest at the poles.
Magnetic force can even work through some materials.
Hold a paper clip under a sheet of paper, and move it with a magnet on top.
It works through water and plastic too. You can rescue a paper clip from a glass of water without getting wet!
Your turn. Where is a magnet's force strongest?
Let's find the strongest magnet.
Hang a paper clip from one pole of a magnet, and add more clips one at a time, in a chain.
Count how many clips the magnet can hold before they fall.
Test different magnets in the same way. The more clips, the stronger the magnet!
Let's remember.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
Opposite poles attract.
Like poles repel.
And the magnetic field is strongest at the poles.
Magnetic work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
